why: A country that never touches the levers panics about as often as the 19th century's large economies did: Britain and the United States had a major crisis about once a decade.
Panics are sharp events, not a permanent state. A moodier market (resting confidence 50) brings a few more panic months: up to 3%.
A panic lasts a season or two, as the historical ones did.
A Mania is rare and memorable.
Many Manias end in a panic, as 1825, 1837, 1847, 1857, 1873 and 1890 did; the rest cool off.
Reckless play costs output over a century compared with careful play, once its rescues and buy-ups are paid for.
Mastery pays: a player who learns the market ends the century richer than one who leaves it alone.
Credit used well beats credit avoided: a player who lets leverage run and reins it in on time out-earns one who never borrows.
Still a challenge: even careful play meets a panic or two a century; skill softens them, it can't abolish them.
Reckless leverage stops the banks: most of a reckless player's panics freeze lending for a while.
Skilled play almost never freezes lending.
Skilled play rarely carries Bad Debts.
And when it does, they are small.
Left alone, Bad Debts clear in a year or two.
Buying up Bad Debts pays for itself: a reckless player who buys them up ends richer than one who never does.
The AI plays the market sensibly: AI countries end at least as rich as one that ignores it, so rivals stay competitive.
A skilled player out-plays the AI at the market.
AI countries have panics about as history did, so Great Powers meet crises and the Long Depression can start.

The Exchange is usually Respected or Trusted: trust is earned in calm years under sound lending and lost in panics, busts and reckless lending, so only a country that keeps losing it sits Doubted or Distrusted.
Careful play keeps the Exchange Respected or better almost all the time.
AI Exchanges are usually Respected or Trusted too, so trust is a normal state and losing it means something.
A hands-off country pays for the leverage it let build: a panic and its Bad Debts cost about a tenth of a year's output, from its start to a year after it ends, as the long slump after 1873 did.
Investment falls hard in a panic: railway investment roughly halved after 1873.
Good years pay: output runs a little above Steady while confidence is Buoyant or in a Mania.
Confidence stays low for a while after a crash, as it did for years after 1837 and 1873: the Wary tier is part of the cycle, not a rarity.
Good years are common but not the norm: Buoyant or Mania about a third of the time.
More advanced finance brings more crashes late in the century, but never a world in constant crisis.
AI countries seldom let their Lending Standards stay Reckless for long.
Some AI governments rescue their banks and some let the panic run, as lenders of last resort spread through the century.
AI panics stop bank lending less often than reckless play does and more often than skilled play.
When an AI country's banks stop lending, it lasts months, not years: nine in ten freezes end within about two years, as in the released game, where the longest ran 36 to 38 months.
